extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (patent attorneys/agents) handling pre‑AIA priority, interference, and related 35 U.S.C. issues
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing priority of invention, derivation, conception, reduction to practice, suppression/ concealment, and related issues under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f)/(g) (interference practice) including interplay with 37 CFR 1.131 and 35 U.S.C. 112/120 requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) does not require an inquiry into the relative dates of a reference and the application, and therefore may be applicable where pre‑AIA subsections (a) and (e) are not available for references having an effective date subsequent to the effective filing date of the application being examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 102(f) addresses derivation (who invented the subject matter). For references dated after the applicant’s effective filing date, evidence may exist that the subject matter was derived from the inventor (or a joint inventor) in view of relative dates; e.g., Ex parte Kusko (215 USPQ 972) — relative dates important in determining derivation; mere listing of authors is not strong evidence to rebut inventor’s declaration of sole inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory standard of pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) bars patent issuance where another inventor made the invention in the United States before the applicant and had not abandoned, suppressed, or concealed it, considering dates of conception and reduction to practice and reasonable diligence of one who was first to conceive and last to reduce to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 102(g) is the statutory basis for interference practice (35 U.S.C. 135, 37 CFR Part 41 Subparts D and E). Priority is determined by conception/reduction to practice dates and diligence; losing party’s subject matter in an interference is rejected under 102(g) unless prior invention acts were not in the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual reduction to practice required for 102(g) prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify as prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) there must be evidence that the subject matter was actually reduced to practice; conception alone is not sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law: Kimberly‑Clark (745 F.2d) — conception without actual reduction insufficient. Filing an application is constructive reduction to practice, but absent evidence of actual reduction (generally not available during ex parte examination) a U.S. patent/application publication falls under 102(e), not 102(g). See In re Zletz (893 F.2d).

rubrics_metrics.name: 102(g) as basis for an ex parte rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) may form the basis for an ex parte rejection if (1) the subject matter was actually reduced to practice by another before the applicant’s invention, and (2) there was no abandonment, suppression, or concealment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities: Amgen v. Chugai; New Idea v. Sperry; E.I. DuPont v. Phillips; Kimberly‑Clark v. Johnson & Johnson. If evidence of actual reduction to practice is lacking, examiner should rely on 102(e) rather than 102(g) for U.S. patent/application references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay of 35 U.S.C. 103(c) with 102(g)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) states that subsection (g) of 102 will not preclude patentability where subject matter developed by another (that would otherwise qualify under 102(g)) and the claimed invention of the application were owned by the same person, subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person, or involved in a qualifying joint research agreement at the time the invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ownership/assignment/joint research agreement conditions of 103(c)(2) and (c)(3) are met, 102(g) does not bar patentability. See MPEP § 2146 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference practice is based on 102(g)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection (g) of pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 is the statutory basis of interference practice for determining priority of invention between parties (inter partes proceedings to determine first to invent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interference involves pending applications and/or unexpired patents naming different inventors; U.S. practice historically emphasizes first to invent in certain applications. Priority time charts and interference principles illustrate when one party is awarded priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of interference outcome on patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon conclusion of an interference, subject matter claimed by the losing party that was the basis of the interference is rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g), unless the acts showing prior invention were not in this country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loss of a count does not automatically make its subject matter statutory prior art for all purposes; however, if the lost count subject matter is available as prior art under 102 it can be used under 103. See In re Deckler (res judicata/collateral estoppel may bar later claims identical to the lost claim).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits vs interference practice
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.131 permits an applicant to show an actual date of invention prior to the effective date of a reference as long as the reference is not a statutory bar under 102(b) or a U.S. patent application publication claiming the same patentable invention; but 37 CFR 1.131 does not apply in interference proceedings which operate to the exclusion of ex parte practice under 1.131.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An application claim to the 'same patentable invention' claimed in a domestic patent requires interference, not an affidavit under 1.131 (Ex parte Standish). Subject matter prior art under 102(g) and subject to an interference is not open to further inquiry under 1.131 during the interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority time chart rules for 1.131 and interference
rubrics_metrics.description: For 37 CFR 1.131 analyses, conception and reduction to practice of the reference to be antedated are considered to be on the effective filing date of a domestic patent application, foreign patent, or date of printed publication; priority time charts illustrate award of priority under various fact patterns (conception, actual reduction, constructive reduction, diligence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charts define C = conception, R = reduction (Ra actual, Rc constructive), TD = commencement of diligence. Examples show when A antedates B or is awarded priority given sequence of conception, actual/constructive reduction, and diligence intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Made in this country requirement for 102(g)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) is available only if made in the United States; acts of conception, reduction to practice and diligence must be demonstrated in this country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 104 and cases (Kondo v. Martel). Knowledge of an invention made abroad and brought into the U.S. may be mere evidence of conception but does not confer the benefit of foreign work unless within NAFTA/WTO rules (dates specified) allowing establishment of invention abroad for interference purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and tests for abandonment, suppression, or concealment
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts hold an invention, though completed, is deemed abandoned, suppressed, or concealed if, within a reasonable time after completion, no steps are taken to make the invention publicly known (e.g., failure to file a patent application, describe in a publicly disseminated document, or use the invention publicly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Correge v. Murphy—filing within 1 year of public disclosure not unreasonable; whether delay constitutes suppression/concealment is fact‑specific. Suppression/concealment can render a de facto later inventor legally first to invent (In re Suska, In re Bass).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference of suppression or concealment from delay in filing
rubrics_metrics.description: During an interference proceeding, an inference of suppression or concealment may arise from an unreasonably long delay in filing a patent application after actual reduction to practice; mere delay alone is not always sufficient—analysis is case‑by‑case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Paulik v. Rizkalla (delay may give rise to inference), Peeler v. Miller (mere delay without more insufficient), Young v. Dworkin (hiatus may give inference). The reasonableness of delay is determined on facts; a long hiatus between reduction to practice and filing can preclude reliance on that earlier reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression or concealment need not be attributed to inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppression or concealment need not be directly attributable to the inventor; delays caused by assignee/employer or counsel may still support an inference of suppression or concealment in an interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peeler v. Miller and Shindelar v. Holdeman show that employer/assignee delays and even patent attorney workload may not excuse unreasonable delays (e.g., four‑year delay by assignee prima facie unreasonable; only short periods like 3 months may be excusable in limited circumstances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebutting inference of suppression or concealment
rubrics_metrics.description: An inference of suppression or concealment is rebuttable if the senior party shows renewed activity on the invention just prior to the junior party’s entry coupled with diligent filing of an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal examples: Holmwood v. Cherpeck—activity directed to perfecting the invention or preparing the application can rebut; Lutzker v. Plet—commercialization activities alone are not sufficient to rebut the inference. The doctrine does not apply to mere conception without actual reduction to practice (Bogoslowsky v. Huse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment distinguished from suppression/concealment
rubrics_metrics.description: A finding of suppression or concealment may not amount to abandonment (loss of right to a patent); an invention cannot be abandoned until it is first reduced to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Steierman v. Connelly; Correge v. Murphy. Distinguish legal consequences of abandonment versus suppression/concealment when assessing rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception: definition and evidentiary requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception is 'the complete performance of the mental part of the inventive act' — formation in the inventor’s mind of a definite and permanent idea of the complete and operative invention as it is thereafter to be applied in practice; must be shown by corroborating evidence and requires possession of every feature recited in the count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: Townsend v. Smith; Hiatt v. Ziegler; Coleman v. Dines; Hybritech v. Monoclonal. Conception requires contemporaneous recognition/appreciation of the invention (Silvestri v. Grant, Invitrogen v. Clontech). Inventor need not know patentability or even be certain the invention will work (Burroughs Wellcome), but mere 'hope' is insufficient (Hitzeman). Conception of a species may not equal conception of the genus or another species; evidence must show every limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception must occur in the inventor's mind and can create joint inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception must be done in the mind of the inventor — a definite and permanent idea — and any person sharing in conception of a claimed invention is a joint inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Bosies v. Benedict; In re VerHoef. Testimony by a noninventor about the meaning of variables in an inventor’s notebook is insufficient to establish conception by the inventor as a matter of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to practice: actual and constructive definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction to practice may be actual (making/using the invention) or constructive (filing a patent application on the claimed invention); the filing of a patent application serves as constructive reduction to practice of subject matter described in the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing an application serves as constructive reduction and can obviate need to provide evidence of conception/actual reduction when relying on the application's content (Hyatt v. Boone). A reduction to practice can be performed by another on the inventor’s behalf (De Solms v. Schoenwald).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive reduction to practice requires compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a)/pre‑AIA 112 and 35 U.S.C. 120 for priority benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: When seeking the benefit of an earlier‑filed U.S. patent application in an interference, the earlier application must meet 35 U.S.C. 120 and 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre‑AIA 112 first paragraph): it must enable and provide a written description of the subject matter of the interference count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of constructive reduction requires sufficient disclosure under 'how to use' and 'how to make' requirements. If the earlier application was abandoned and not co‑pending (or fails 120/112), its filing may be evidence only of conception, not constructive reduction (In re Costello). Kawai v. Metlesics: constructive reduction not proven unless specification discloses practical utility where not obvious.
